title.en: The House of Darkness and the Fireflies

region.en: Xibalba (the place of fear), symbolic pin at the Candelaria caves, Guatemala highlands
region.zh: 希巴爾巴（懼地），以危地馬拉高地坎德拉里亞洞群為象徵定位

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 3, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: The twins are given the second trial their fathers failed: keep a red cigar and a pitch torch burning through the night in the House of Darkness. Instead of lighting them, they fix a red-feathered firefly to each — and at dawn, having burned nothing, they are alive and the game goes on.
summary.zh: 雙子遭遇其父失敗的同一試煉：須於黑暗之屋中，令紅雪茄與松脂火把徹夜不熄。他們不點燃真火，而以兩隻紅羽螢火蟲充之——黎明時火未燃而人未死，賽事繼續。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The lords of the place of fear are delighted: these are the players who will die as their fathers did. On the first night they are shut in the House of Darkness, and a red cigar and a stick of pitch are set before them with the order to keep them whole and burning until morning, without consuming them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: The twins do nothing of the kind: they set a firefly on the tip of the cigar and another on the end of the torch, and the glow and motion of the red-flies deceive the watchers in the dark. All night the watchers see the lights moving and burning, and the twins lie down unburned.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: At dawn the cigar and the stick are brought out whole, unlit, and the lords are furious and confused. 'Who brought these in? Where did they come from? They look like us.' The twins have passed the first house, and the lords begin to suspect they are not boys at all but something beyond their tricks.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.

title.zh: 利刃、嚴寒與美洲豹之屋

region.en: Xibalba (the place of fear), symbolic pin at the Candelaria caves, Guatemala highlands
region.zh: 希巴爾巴（懼地），以危地馬拉高地坎德拉里亞洞群為象徵定位

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 3, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: Night after night the houses try them: the House of Razors, whose blades the twins talk into gathering up their edges; the House of Cold, kept off with old pine knots; the House of Jaguars, whose teeth they feed with the bones of other animals. Each morning they walk out whole and cheerful.
summary.zh: 夜復一夜，諸屋試煉他們：利刃之屋——雙子以言語令利刃自行收攏鋒芒；嚴寒之屋——以陳年松柴御寒；美洲豹之屋——以獸骨餵其利齒。每個清晨，他們完好而歡愉地走出。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Next is the House of Razors, full of blades that move on their own, the razors that belong to Xibalba. But the twins speak to them: 'Yours are the bones; ours is the flesh.' And the razors stand down and gather themselves up and keep quiet in the corners, so the boys sleep soundly among their edges.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then comes the House of Cold, where the frozen wind kills whoever lies in it; they warm themselves with pine knots saved from the woodpile, old ones, and pass the night. After it, the House of Jaguars, loud with cats that bite; but the twins scatter the bones of other animals for them and feed them what jaguars like, and the cats are content and do not touch the boys.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: Each morning the lords come to look, hoping for bones, and each morning the twins walk out undamaged, laughing among themselves. The houses are failing one by one, and the Lords of Xibalba begin to play for the end: the House of Bats, which no one has survived.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.

title.en: The House of Bats: Camazotz Snips Off a Head
title.zh: 蝙蝠之屋：卡馬佐茲剪首

region.en: Xibalba (the place of fear), symbolic pin at the Candelaria caves, Guatemala highlands
region.zh: 希巴爾巴（懼地），以危地馬拉高地坎德拉里亞洞群為象徵定位

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 3, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: In the House of Bats the twins hide inside their blowguns while the death bats cut the air. At noon Camazotz comes down looking for the dawn; Hunahpu peeks out, and his head is snipped off. Xbalanque calls the animals for help, and the tortoise and the daykeepers fashion a new head — the boy goes out with a squash for a face.
summary.zh: 蝙蝠之屋中，雙子藏身於吹箭筒內，死亡蝙蝠在空中剪掠。正午卡馬佐茲下來尋覓黎明；烏納普探頭而出，頭顱隨即被剪。斯巴蘭克召集獸眾求助，烏龜與日守者為其塑新首——男孩以葫蘆為面而出。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The House of Bats is a cave of knives on wings. The twins crawl inside their blowguns and wait while the bats slice the dark, and Xbalanque says: look after your head, brother, and keep still. The bats circle all night, cutting the air where the boys breathe.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: At noon Camazotz comes down to look for the light. Hunahpu lifts his head from the tube to see whether the dawn has come, and the great bat's snipping blades take it off like a ripe fruit. The head rolls away, and the body in the tube does not move again that day. Xbalanque calls the animals: coati, coyote, all of you come, and they gather and bring the head before the Lords of Xibalba, who are overjoyed at the loss.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: But Xbalanque does not grieve: he sets a turtle on his brother's neck and the daykeepers shape the shell into a face, and then a round squash is brought in from the cornfield and painted like a head, and Hunahpu is given that to wear. He goes out at the next muster with his squash face among the lords, who laugh at the two poor boys and do not understand what has been rebuilt in the House of Bats.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The House of Bats is the one trial in Xibalba that the Hero Twins cannot charm, and it nearly ends the cycle. Popol Wuj places it last among the terrible houses of the place of fear, after Darkness, Razors, Cold, and Jaguars — a descending sequence toward the house whose guardian, Camazotz (Snatch Bat, the Death Bat), is not a lord in the council but a killer animal waiting overhead.

The twins enter by order of the Lords of Xibalba, who are now desperate: every trap has failed. In the bat house the darkness is full of wings that cut. Hunahpu and Xbalanque take shelter inside their blowguns, which in Maya ballgame iconography are the emblem of the game and its players; hiding inside the instrument of their art, they wait out the night. Xbalanque warns his brother: do not lift your head until the light comes; watch over yourself. The advice matters because the bats here are hunting, and their targets are heads.

At noon — a chilling inversion, since noon is when the sun is highest and should be safest — Camazotz comes down from the roof, looking for the dawn. Hunahpu peeks out to see if the day has arrived, and the bat severs his head in one cut. In the K'iche' text the bat snips it 'from off his body', and the head rolls in the dark. Xbalanque calls the animals of the earth — the coati and the others — and they bring the head into the open, where the Lords of Xibalba, seeing it, rejoice: at last one of the two is dead.

What follows is the quiet countermove. Xbalanque does not mourn. He summons the daykeepers (the grandmother and grandfather figures of the tradition) and sets a tortoise against his brother's neck; the shell is shaped into a face, and over it goes a squash from the cornfield, painted like a head. When the lords next muster the brothers for the ballgame, Hunahpu stands among them with his squash face, and the Lords of Xibalba laugh at the poor boys, not realizing that the boy they killed has been put together again out of turtle shell and gourd. The episode's cultural function is double: it marks the absolute limit of trickery — there are powers (Camazotz, noon, the bat's blade) that cannot be talked into mercy — and it shows the method of the twins' whole victory, which is never to fight the underworld at strength but to treat each loss as material for reconstruction. The reassembled Hunahpu, his head a painted gourd, is one of the most recognizable images of Maya narrative: the hero whose face is provisional and who therefore cannot be finished off.

functions: Marks the limit of the twins' trickery: death itself is suffered, not avoided
Models resurrection through substitution (turtle shell, painted squash), a motif of Maya funerary art
Justifies noon as the hour when death-bats (and, by extension, household taboos on noon naps) are dangerous

variants.name: Xibalba as the Candelaria cave complex
variants.text_tradition: Archaeological identifications of Xibalba's road systems with the Candelaria caves (Guatemala lowland-highland border)
variants.summary: Some scholars read the rivers, crossings, and dark houses of Popol Wuj as a description of a real cave system; the bat house matches bat colonies in deep chambers.

variants.name: Classic-period ceramic bat imagery
variants.text_tradition: Late Classic polychrome vessels (e.g., the 'Cosmic Plate' and bat-headed lords)
variants.summary: Bat-headed figures and the 'flying' death-bat appear on Classic Maya vessels, suggesting the Camazotz episode's iconography predates the colonial text.

title.en: Ground to Powder, Cast in the River

region.en: Xibalba (the place of fear), symbolic pin at the Candelaria caves, Guatemala highlands
region.zh: 希巴爾巴（懼地），以危地馬拉高地坎德拉里亞洞群為象徵定位

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 3, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: At the lords' final request the twins stage their own deaths: they grind each other's bones in a mortar and pour them into the river. From the ground bones they reappear — first as catfish, then as boys again — and resume their dances in the council hall, apparently none the worse.
summary.zh: 應冥主最後所求，雙子自導死亡：於臼中互碾其骨，傾入河中。碎骨化形重現——初為鯰魚，復為男孩——回到議事堂中起舞，看似毫髮無損。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The lords send for the twins and ask for the miracle plainly: we want to see you die and come back. The brothers answer that it is easy. Then they arrange everything and stand together in the court, and they drop down dead at the same moment, in front of all the benches.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: The lords are overjoyed; but they are also uneasy, and they take the bodies to a large mortar and grind them to powder, bones and all, and pour the ground bone and meal into the river. The river carries it off, and the lords think the matter finished — the players are nothing but water.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the fifth day two boys appear in the river as young catfish, and the next day as boys again, and they walk back into the hall of Xibalba in the clothes of their dance, keeping their faces down. The lords do not know them. They ask for the dance, and the boys say: we are the little dancers; give us the fire.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.

title.en: The Dance of the Poor Sufferer

region.en: Xibalba (the place of fear), symbolic pin at the Candelaria caves, Guatemala highlands
region.zh: 希巴爾巴（懼地），以危地馬拉高地坎德拉里亞洞群為象徵定位

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 3, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: As entertainers the twins burn the lords' house with themselves inside and step out unharmed; they sacrifice a dog and restore it; they cut each other apart and reassemble. The Lords of Xibalba, watching, are carried away — and ask to be shown the dance of death as well.
summary.zh: 雙子扮作藝者，與房屋同焚而毫髮無傷走出；獻祭犬隻又使其復原；互剖其身而復合。冥主觀之入迷——進而求觀死亡之舞。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The twins perform. They set fire to a house with themselves inside and dance out of the flames unhurt; they kill a dog and bring it back to life; they cut themselves open, take out their hearts, and put them back, and go on dancing. Each trick is announced by the one who is about to die, who tells the other, and then it is done.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: The lords of the place of fear are beside themselves. They crowd the benches to watch, calling for more: kill each other, burn yourselves, do it again. The twins oblige with faces of sorrow and feats of laughter, until One Death and Seven Death themselves begin to boast: if the boys can die and return, so can the Lords of Death.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: And so they ask for their turn, which is exactly what the twins have danced toward. The boys tell them: it is right that it should be tried, and the lords prepare to die in front of everyone, certain of their resurrection, having watched two boys do it three times without harm.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.

title.en: Sacrifice Without Resurrection: One Death and Seven Death Die
title.zh: 有祭無復：一死神與七死神之死

region.en: Xibalba (the place of fear), symbolic pin at the Candelaria caves, Guatemala highlands
region.zh: 希巴爾巴（懼地），以危地馬拉高地坎德拉里亞洞群為象徵定位

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 3, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: The senior lords demand the twins' dance of death for themselves. The twins open their chests, take out their hearts, and revive — but when One Death and Seven Death are sacrificed the same way, the boys do not revive them. The two great lords die in front of their court, and the lesser lords confess and submit.
summary.zh: 兩位首主求觀雙子的死亡之舞，欲親身一試。雙子剖胸取心而復生——然當一死神與七死神以同法受祭時，男孩們卻不令其復原。兩大主死於其廷前，餘主俯首認罪。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The twins tell the two senior lords: dance your death; it is proper. One Death and Seven Death come forward to the middle of the court, and their hearts are taken out, and they are opened like the boys were — and this time the boys do not put anything back and do not say the word that restores.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: The two lords die before all their bench of underlords, and the court cries out for them to be brought back. The twins answer mildly: they were tricked by the dance, as they tricked others; they wanted what they saw. And the remaining lords, Pus, Blood, Bone Scepter, Wing, and the rest, come in a body to confess and to offer whatever the boys demand.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: The twins spare the lesser lords but strip them of their emblems and their court: they will no longer be named in order of their cruelties, and their power over the ballgame and over men's hearts is taken. They confess their sins — the failures of hospitality, the deaths of players — and from then on they carry out only the small offices of the place of fear, no longer its judgments.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The defeat of One Death and Seven Death is the climax of the Hero Twins' cycle and the most juridical scene in the Popol Wuj: a trial that reverses itself. The two boys, having survived every house and risen twice from their own staged deaths, have by now converted the underworld's justice hall into a theater, and the theater into a trap. The Lords of Xibalba, who opened the cycle by summoning two ballplayers to a rigged game, now beg two ballplayers for one last spectacle — and the spectacle is their own execution, performed in the form they themselves designed: death on demand, resurrection on demand.

The sequence is deliberately simple. Hunahpu and Xbalanque, asked to repeat their wonders, kill themselves again — this time before the full court — and come back dancing. One Death and Seven Death, senior lords of the council of the dead, are so persuaded by repetition that they volunteer: if boys can die and return, surely the masters of death can. The twins consent with perfect courtesy and perfect honesty ('it is proper that it be tried') and then simply decline the last step. When the lords' hearts are out, the boys do not speak the word of restoration; they leave the two great lords dead on the floor of their own hall. There is no trick in the death itself — only in the promise of its reversal, which was never made.

The lesser lords then do what courts do when their heads are gone: they confess. In the K'iche' text they come in a body, admitting the deaths of the players, the abuse of guests, and the theft of the ballgame, and they offer submission. The twins respond not with massacre but with demotion: the remaining lords of Xibalba are kept as functionaries of death — they will still receive the dead, but without the emblems of judgment, without the power to summon the living, and stripped of the titles by which their cruelties were remembered. Death is not abolished; it is domesticated. From this point on, Xibalba is a place where people go, not a power that comes to fetch people by trick summons.

Ritually, the episode licenses the Maya practice of sacrifice as negotiation rather than submission: blood is given because a covenant can be made, not because the underworld's whims must be bought. Politically, it authorizes the K'iche' ballgame and its courts as places where disputes are settled by rules rather than ambush — the twins win by knowing the rules better than the house does. And theologically, it grounds the calendar: the twins' final transformation into sun and moon (elsewhere in the record) rests on this victory over the lords of the katun's dark days.

functions: Climax of the twins' cycle: the reversal of the underworld's court
Licenses sacrifice as covenant with the gods rather than tribute to death
Explains why the dead are received but no longer summoned: Xibalba's demotion
Authorizes the ballgame as a rule-bound settlement of contests

variants.name: Broad arc in the single-record tradition
variants.summary: The whole Xibalba defeat is often told as one story ('the Hero Twins in Xibalba'); this record cuts its final, juridical scene.

title.en: The Twins Ascend: Sun, Moon, and the Four Hundred Boys
title.zh: 雙子昇天：日、月與四百男孩

region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 3, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: Having cleared the world of false suns and defeated the lords of death, Hunahpu and Xbalanque rise into the sky — one as the sun, one as the moon — lighting the earth for the first time. The Four Hundred Boys who died with Zipacna rise with them as the stars of the Pleiades.
summary.zh: 清除偽日、擊敗死神諸主之後，烏納普與斯巴蘭克昇入天空——一為太陽，一為月亮——首次照亮大地。與希帕克納同死的四百男孩隨之昇為昴宿之星。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Then the two boys rise, not by stairs or by rope but simply, into the middle of the light: one becomes the sun and the other the moon. The face of the earth is lit for the first time, and the valleys and canyons are clear under them. And the Four Hundred Boys, who died in the house of Zipacna, go up with them and become the stars, the Four Hundred scattered in the sky on clear nights.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: Thus the count of days begins under a true sun, with no counterfeit light and no lord able to summon the living by ambush. What the twins did in the place of fear is retold at the rising of each new sun, and the dawn is called the raising of their faces.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.

title.en: The Grandmother's Loom and the Five Faces
title.zh: 祖母的織機與五度面容

region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 3, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: Waiting below for the twins' rising, Xmucane weaves at her loom, and the faces of the two boys appear in the weave of the cloth five times — then vanish with the fifth. She understands: her grandsons are in the sky now, and the loom holds their memory.
summary.zh: 徐穆坎在下方織布等候雙子昇天，男孩的面容在織物經緯間五度浮現——至第五次隨之隱沒。她明白了：孫子們已在天空，而織機留存其形貌。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Xmucane keeps watch below, weaving, while her grandsons do their work in the sky. In the cloth she weaves, the faces of the two boys come and go: she sees them once, twice, three times, and at the fifth appearance they are gone, and the weave is only cloth.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: She sets down her work and understands what has happened: the twins are finished with the earth and are in the light now, and whatever she weaves afterward will hold only their memory. This is why the weaver's loom is a place of remembering in the houses of the K'iche', and why the count of days keeps the faces of the ancestors.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.
